If you want to charge more than $499, you can't call it the "7-class" of the series.

Author: @AdvanceWars
Content:
I've been thinking about how AMD could come out on top of NVIDIA and only came up with bring back CrossFire. Hear me out, please!

Make a mid tier card that get's people in the door. If a consumer decides, "Hey, I wanna upgrade! But I don't want to have to sell this mid tier and hope I get half back to at least put to the newer one." Well, that's where the whole CrossFire can come in. They can just buy another of the same card and use it in a way that mimics a full on $1000

AMD is already content with making mid tier, compared to NVIDIA. And I'm not saying they shouldn't make a card on par with NVIDIA, but I would love to be able to start a build with 1 card at $500-$750 and then later on get the same model for cheaper AND a better experience. There's just too much focus on 1 great card that must have the latest and greatest that it sucks when said card costs $1000+ and is burning cables. And not really to spec.

I never really used CrossFire or SLI, I really only used 1 card each build I had, but I think there were issues with both systems. If AMD can step up and make it work at 100% or at least 95% of NVIDIA's newest card, I'd be on board with them all the way. Right now I'm still with my RTX 2080 and I might not upgrade till I know a new card is worth it.

I've seen plenty of people talk about AMD and Intel needing to step up their game to compare to NVIDIA, and I'm right there with them. But besides "Make a better or on par GPU" I haven't heard about what they could do with mid tier. 

Anyway, my 2 cents. Thanks for reading.

Author: @BeardedFrog
Content:
Maybe I'm just a pessimist but I don't think there is anything AMD can do at this point to "save" us. Additionally, in the current state of things, _availability_ ,not pricing is going to be the most important thing for AMD. 

Currently Nvidia is messing up in all these ways, but at the end of the day, they're still selling more cards then they can make right now. Whether a 50 series card costs $50 or $5,000 is irrelevant when they aren't _actually_ there to buy (outside of scalpers). They aren't losing any money on these issues with power connectors, black screen, missing rops, etc, only on availability.

If availability wasn't an issue for Nvidia, and the 50 series cards were readily available to buy, then these issues might have actually hurt Nvidia. Then if AMD had a successful launch without issues, you MIGHT see people switching. This isn't the case though right now. The biggest factor for people needing to buy a GPU right now is simply... "Where can I even get one without paying a scalper?"

So if AMD wants a successful launch, they just need to be armed with scalper proof level of stock available to do so.

That said the real pessimistic (but likely sadly realistic) fact is that this is only going to get worse.

Nvidia has not only 90% of the market share but also a TON more capital/ability. They are making a killing in the AI space, and their AI based cards have perfect synergy with their consumer "gamer" cards. AMD doesn't have this, nor does Intel (at least not on that level). They make way more money there, and barely need to even care at all about us "gamers." Comparing Nvidia's technology level and ability to AMD and Intel is like comparing companies that are a decade apart in time. Nvidia is way ahead here.

AMD can claim they stopped targeting the high end market by choice because of profit margins, but the reality is they have _no actual ability_ to compete at that level against Nvidia anymore since Nvidia became this dominant force in AI.

Additionally, whether you are a customer wanting a top tier card or a budget card, having Nvidia being the only one making top tier cards, and thus dominating charts at the top end has a _massive_ effect on the reputation appearance. When you see a chart and the top half of the chart is all one company it has an effect on the mindset of buyers at all levels.

TLDR: AMD's only path to making a difference is going to be if they ACTUALLY have cards for sale, and ACTUALLY near MSRP. However, for gamers this stuff is only going to get worse, and we will continually become more of a slave to Nvidia as they continue to grow further and further apart from AMD and Intel in technological advancement.

Author: @n3rdcom
Content: Here's the problem with this logic of undercutting really heavily: It ignores AMD's cost. They have to report to shareholders about profits on these products, and if they're not making a certain profit margin or even losing money, the shareholders and board are going to vote to cut their R&D budget in the GPU division. This ultimately means they're just going to fall further behind, and then we lose them even trying to compete at the mid-range level. They've already been disincentivized from trying to compete at the top end because of the costs. We have NO IDEA what their cost is on these new GPUs or what the AIB partners' margins are either and the AIB's have a final say in the pricing as well. What we DO KNOW that TSMC's wafer cost is going up consistently and no amount of consumer intervention is going to change this. I'm all for the pro-consumer sentiment, but we can only fight the realities to a certain extent. As much as I would love to see a 9070 XT under $600 it just may not be realistic not only in the short term but it could have worse long-term repercussions. I want to be clear that I'm not defending the pricing by any means, just rationalizing what it might look like from the other side of the coin. Also, the enthusiast market may not give a single f*ck about what AMD has to offer regardless. There may be so many that are in the "Charge me more Nvidia daddy" camp that even if the 9070 XT comes out at the price of $1 it may not move the needle the slightest bit in the overall market share.

Author: @EndermanEatBlocks
Content:
If you make Indygames, and some AMD specific shader-bullshit pops up, you can just refund ~500 people, before you break even with buying/building a AMD test machine. 
The sad truth of steam in 2025 is that it needs to work on GTX10xx and RTX20xx, the rest is only relevant for 0,01% of games. And those games can pay for the support AND break even on that decision. Could I swap graphics cards in my rig to test? Sure, but I won't. I MAYBE test on integrated, if I feel like it.

AMD is in the position where even large companies just test in their cards a few weeks before releasing or a few days before pushing an update. And if fancy-rendering-feature does not work on their cards it just gets disabled. You will be better off releasing earlier.

Its not bad hardware, its just not relevant enough to be even planned for. In a world with 3 companies, having below 20% puts you in that feedbackloop they went in 5 years ago.

Content:
I think AMD is vastly underestimating how many people are still sitting on old or super cheap hardware like me. $700 for just a GPU, is actively pricing me out of the modern era of this hobby.
This isn't even their compute GPU line-up, so you can't make the same statements that people will about NVIDIA and AI research. Leaks say that UDNA is apparently coming, for what that's worth, but right now, RDNA was built more for gaming and not compute. So them trying to prop up the idea that it's worth so much more, when probably a good 80% of that 10% market-share, are probably just people looking to play games and do simple creative work.

If they want customers, they need to accept the current market and take a smaller margin for a massively higher sales volume.

Their drivers have literally gone from "sometimes it blue-screens your computer, on a fresh Windows install, just because you told it to install", to "It recovers itself if it crashes even from user fault, and almost always recovers". They have put in so much work to make their hardware be a good experience and they almost always seem to mess up the pricing.

Time for round... 5? 6? Eh, whatever, the market-share numbers say it all, really.

Author: @Kamyar-fm3jh
Content:
I know this won't get an answer but I really like to ask you to consider how I see it. I'd love to gain some understanding 

IMHO, AMD dropping prices on its GPUs just doesn't add up. They're already churning out every chip they can make—ramping up production isn’t an overnight switch, it's a process that takes years and massive investments. Lower prices would just ignite a surge in demand that their fabs can't meet, further straining an already tight supply chain that's fully committed to higher-margin areas like AI, servers, and crypto.

And here's another kicker: in a decade or more, the consumer gaming PC market might be nothing more than a nostalgic footnote. With cloud gaming taking off and major players shifting their focus away from traditional PCs, why would AMD try to carve out market share in a segment that's gradually becoming obsolete? Their current strategy of targeting markets with sustainable, long-term growth is a smarter play than chasing a market that’s already on its way out.

Author: @JheregJAB
Content: For AMD to compete with Nvidia, I think they need to do two things. First, recognize that no casual observer who wants a high-performance card even really looks at them right now. They are missing too many features that nvidia has, and they just keep playing catch-up. If they want market share, they should price their cards in such a way that you look at a mid-range nvidia card, and the high-tier AMD is better priced. Let the raw benchmark numbers be better for the price by a lot, and the consumer will care less about the missing features. Second, they need to put together some kind of (separate) competing AI graphics card. Price it like a 5090, but give it triple the graphics ram. Suddenly nvidia won't be the only name you think of when thinking about LLMs, and there is a real chance there to steal market share.

Author: @chexo3
Content:
Radeon also has an opportunity with the increasing market share of Linux in the gaming space: not just by nerds like myself who either switched from Windows years ago or have wanted to switch for years and finally did recently

That opportunity is simple: their Linux drivers aren’t a massive pain in the ass. They work *with* the Linux kernel community, not against them, and so they don’t get pissed off Torvalds swearing at them, and when you boot up a Linux installer image/ISO, your Radeon card would just work because the drivers aren’t being developed out-of-tree like Nvidia’s.

Linux is exactly why I want to buy a Radeon card. Because switching from Windows has become necessary, and everything about it has been great except owning an Nvidia GPU. I’m not going to act like it hasn’t gotten better with Nvidia cards under Linux, but that’s more a case of Nvidia being dragged kicking and screaming to care about Linux servers, and for desktop use cases distributions have picked up the slack with home grown Nvidia driver installation tools.

So anyways, I hope AMD prices cards competitively because I *want* to rid myself of the frustration of owning an Nvidia card while using Linux.

If you study intergenerational pricing, you'll find that AMD uses the predecessor of the same performance level, adds about $100 because its a new product, and then adds or subtracts $150 for every 8GB difference in VRAM. The RX 9070 XT is approx. as fast the RX 7900 XTX rasterized, and prior the price hikes sold for around $900. If you do the math, then the resulting price would be around $850 - which apparently is the price AMD targeted prior to learning about the RTX 4070 Ti at $750 MSRP.
Now the new price is rumored to be around $750 as well, and the only reason that might sell is because you can't actually get an RTX 4070 Ti for $750 but $1050 instead.
AMD complained about bad RDNA 3 sales except that was their own fault and due to unfriendly pricing, which is unsurprising since even RDNA 2 got you better performance per buck.

Intel showed us that a 12GB is required and it should be around $250, but selling a GPU about twice that performance and +4GB VRAM for over $550 ? That simply won't fly.

Content:
While I agree with Steve that AMD need customers more than money now, I disagree with the idea that they should sell GPUs dirt-cheap. If AMD doesn't make money they would not have money to invest in further research and development of their GPUs. That would mean they would be even worse compared to NVidia, and thus nobody would want to buy it (to put it shortly: nobody buys sh1t no matter how cheap it is).

To me it seems like AMD need to find a fine line between "dirt-cheap" prices and "NVidia - 50 USD" if that is possible. They need to make enough, but not more than that.

Author: @bslay4r
Content:
They have to sell the cards with higher margin because as a company you can't let one product division drag down the average profit margin of the whole company. It's around 50% (GAAP) for the whole company but only ~20-25% at the gaming division so it's already very low in comparison to the whole industry. 
This video won't make a difference at AMD because this is not about consumers anymore but about quarterly earnings. Their market share with the integrated GPUs and the consoles is already very high so the (market share of the) desktop space is not important anymore. It's a low number in sales volume and even lower in margins.

So no, they won't change their tactics.
This is how the stock market works, short term profits over longer term visions. This type of "behavior" caused some companies to fail or to shrink (Intel is one of them) but most can make this work.

Author: @Stephen__White
Content:
The frustrating thing for me as a 6700 XT owner, is that I honestly could not give two shits about AMD having their own version of Shadowplay, if I want to record something I've got OBS open and I'm already recording it. I couldn't give two shits about FSR or really up-scaling in general, I'd rather just have a GPU that works without needing to use some software to adjust the resolution for me. I couldn't give a shit about Anti-Lag, I don't use it nor do I really see the point to it, if you are having issues of latency in games solve it yourself. If it's your internet connection causing online latency issues, get a better internet package. If it's your peripherals are shit and very high latency... get better peripherals! The biggest one I couldn't give a shit about is Frame Generation/Fluid Motion Frames, as stated earlier, I want a GPU that I know JUST WORKS. No fancy bells and whistles, you just pop it in, and you can trust that it can play any modern game at a minimum of high settings with no level of up-scaling/frame generation needed unless the game itself is just shit and poorly optimized. 

I paid around $450 Canadian for my 6700 XT. At the time it was a toss up between it and a 6800 non-XT for $600 and I went with the 6700 XT so I could put that extra $150 into other parts of my PC build. Given what I bought was an Intel CPU that has since been retired because it was 13th gen and showing clear signs of degrading.(performance loss, random crashing the works) I do kind of wish I had spent the little extra on the GPU, but that's beside the point. 

My main point is, AMD needs to stop trying to be a little Nvidia. They don't need to be, they only need to be AMD. They need to be the company that says to hell with all this extra fancy crap that no one cares about, and make GPUs that have amazing raster performance. Force Nvidia to have to use frame gen to beat their cards, force Nvidia to keep pumping more and more raw power into their GPUs while AMD focuses on pure raster performance and power efficiency, and they will topple Nvidia just like they did Intel on the CPU front. AMD for the love of god, find your GPU gimmick, something akin to X3D but for GPUs. The 9000 series is perfect for that type of experimenting. Find the price floor you can go to and make a solid line up of cards for that price floor. Set a hard price cap to keep all products under, something like $649.99 being the tippy top end for AMD made GPUs, they can't exactly control partner model pricing but they can control their own.

I'll stop my ramble now, I just want AMD to be better so I actually have something to upgrade into, because I refuse to buy Nvidia and have a major fire risk sitting next to me. Hope anyone who reads my ramble is having a nice day!

Author: @zues121510
Content:
I will look forward to buying the 40 or 50 series Nvidia cards used for a normal person price in 3-5 years it seems (like $300). AMD isn't even an option where I live because they're so rare there's no competition on ebay for them and the new prices are not something i can swallow, so i can get a significantly better deal later. I even *_wanted_*_ to upgrade to a new AMD card_ because I remember them being a good value when I first built my PC and i heard some stuff about the value being good on AMD cards, but I didn't realise that was only relatively speaking and I'd have to cough up like £400 for any significant upgrade over my almost decade old card.

It's like AMD is actively trying to convince me to not give them my money and give it to Nvidia's customers on eBay instead, because I literally wanted to give it to them but couldn't because of a lack of a compelling upgrade option for a normal price. Nvidia cards are literally way cheaper used whilst having all the benefits that AMD doesn't like DLSS which are basically necessary because of how poorly optimized games are now, so my purchase decision was in part decided by this sadly. 

I upgraded from my 1070ti to a used 3070 that was much cheaper than the few used AMD equivalents being sold at the time on ebay (the 3070 had like 300 GPUs being sold at once, most AMD cards were in the single digits) last year. The closest new AMD card to the 3070 in performance was the 7700xt, they performed the same but the 7700xt cost *double* what the used 3070 went for, consumed more power and didn't have the compelling features like DLSS. The 7600xt was still out of my price point, being 20% slower than the used 3070 but costing 50% more. The only thing at my price point was the entry level 7600, but there was no point in upgrading to it because it wasn't even much of an upgrade over my 7 year old mid-range card (1070 ti), with it barely having a double digit increase whilst consuming just a few watts less of power, so it didn't even have efficiency going for it. Back when I got my previous card, an Nvidia card at the 7600xt price point would match or outperform the previous generation $1000 Titan, the highest end card, and consume much less power, but now AMD after almost a decade gives us a measly 10-20% gain over a mid-range card whilst consuming almost the same power. This is what riding Nvidia's Weiner Nut gets you AMD! I can't even buy AMD used because nobody even buys the cards new now, let alone give the money to AMD directly. 

I AM LITERALLY ASKING A BILLION DOLLAR COMPANY TO LET ME GIVE THEM MY MONEY. I THOUGHT IT WAS *THEIR* JOB TO DO THIS?!?! 
...Pattern the fuck up AMD

Also I'd like to mention that I paid more the market average for the 3070 because the guy still had the original receipt, warranty was still intact, the plastic wrap was still on the shroud and the guy said he barely even used the thing, and this price is what i am using for the metric.

Author: @SvalbardSleeperDistrict
Content:
At the end of the day, the core of the situation we're in is in history. It's not about whether Nvidia's X GPU in Y year was better than AMD's, etc, it's the fact that Nvidia ended up where it is by decades of deeply unethical, borderline illegal monopolistic practices against partners, competitors and users. Threatening partners, undermining competitors with shady dealing behind the scenes, and shafting users. And that is what the late-stage neoliberal capitalist market rewards - it does not reward being a more honest company, or pricing your products more fairly for users. And when both the market and users kept rewarding Nvidia for those practices, the outcome was always inevitable - you get so much money from gradually gobbling up market share that you can afford more R&D, you can afford multiple-pronged development your competitors can't keep up with, you can afford to flood retail stores with your GPUs in the way they cannot, and so on. 

The solutions are, as always, systemic and political - there needs to be strict, daily, unrelenting regulation and punishment of companies like this one, for there to be any chance of a fair and user-centric market.

If AMD adopts fair pricing, similar to when they were selling FX processors (back when Intel was far ahead of them), they could generate revenue and stage a comeback, just like they did with Ryzen taking the competition by surprise.

At this point, even many NVIDIA fanboys don’t want to buy a GPU from them due to their pricing.

Additionally, if AMD finds a way to prevent scalpers and ensures that end consumers can buy GPUs at MSRP, it would make a huge difference.

A lot of people just want to play games and don’t care about extra FPS. Many are still holding onto RX 480 and RX 580 cards simply because of GPU pricing. (I was in the same situation myself until I bought a second-hand 6700 XT for €150.)

Author: @durentis
Content:
Very well said. 

I bought what was expected to be a very temporary B580 LE for CAD$359. My thought process at the time was to await 5090 stock to game at 4K, to not support Nvidia's paper launch by buying another of their cards in the meantime, to not support AMD for backing out from high end competitive cards, and (more positively) to actively support Intel for stepping up and knocking it out of the park in the budget not-4K space. (I don't recognize a middle space.)

Nvidia's power plane design crashing and burning like a Boeing under Delta, all else sadly forgivable, has forced me to stay within the not-4K space for the foreseeable future. 

This puts AMD in a very tough spot, from my perspective, because they not only have to produce an actually good 5070 Ti to compete a level up from the B580, they have to actually justify the jump up from the B580 despite staying in the not-4K space. And good luck with that.. the B580 LE gets it done. I feel this pulls their ideal price down, value-wise far below what they would like or may even be profitable. 

Or, you know, AMD could just surprise us with a competitive card in the 4K space after all. I think they have one very small window of opportunity to recover customers here.

Nvidia has engineered such comical prices at this point that it can probably afford to come back to near official MSRP and still make a profit.  So AMD will be a price-taker no matter what it does.

Content: 29:49  AMD should quite literally price these at 1% margins. Cost plus 1%. They're not going to. But that's what they should do. The reality is that it will take two to three generations for AMD to correct its disastrous last 10-15 years. They're going to have to pour money into this, so they shouldn't be losing money on a per card basis, but they should absolutely be looking at no more than 1% profit per card. And they're just going to have to live with the fact that it's going to take at least two generations of that, before they see a real inroad. They can absolutely gain this year, this generation, in market share if they execute correctly right now, but that won't be sufficient for mind share. They have to do this for the next generation too. And the next generation they absolutely need to have something in the 80 category. It does not have to be better than whatever the 80 tier from Nvidia is going to be, and performance, what it needs to be is significantly cheaper and give near equivalent capability. But that's the next generation, this generation they need to focus on 1% profit and only 1%. And crank them out by the hundreds of thousands. It does not matter if they have so many that the next generation will be competing with it, because the next generation will also be at 1%. But should also have an 80 tier. And both generations need to have spec-wise, sufficient VRAM to satisfy the customer

Author: @SherrifOfNottingham
Content:
The markup on these cards is so out of control that they don't want to actually release a price competitive card because it will shatter the illusion.

The fact is if the 9070 xt (which is performance comparative to the 4070 ti) selling for a competitive price would be around 350 bucks, anything higher and it's going to be an "upsell" sku for 4070 ti's. AMD needs to remember that the 'edge' Nvidia has (or is supposed to have) is that consumer confidence, that consumers are guaranteed it will work with their games, won't have weird crashes or bugs. Many people will easily pay 200 bucks more for that confidence, at 300 you're at least in the range of the upsell sku being a big enough of a gap to be considered. Even lower would be remarkably better at convincing people to stick with your sku.

The problem AMD is having is they know the sad reality of selling these cards for the right price, the previous years cards are going to collapse. Retailers are going to struggle to move inventory of the overpriced cards now that consumers see the "real" pricing show up. AMD is afraid of the consequences of doing this because they're afraid retailers aren't going to want to buy future cards.

But here's the thing... retailers aren't stupid, they're more likely to stop carrying your cards simply because the market share is that bad. AMD should adopt the "NVidia but half" formula for now, getting cards in people's hands, capturing that market share is far more important than anything else, even short term profits at this point.

Author: @AbsolutTalent1
Content:
Just throwing out my opinion, which isnt worth much. Previously I always had a hard set limit of maybe 200-300max to spend on a video card. I always targeted the mid range for builds. Right around the start of the first round of mining craze, when I was looking at building a new system with the brand new Ryzens, i was set on either the rx480 or the 1060 6gb. I ended up going with the 1060 because it was in stock and a little cheaper at the time at my local Microcenter. I thought it served me well, but flash forward to when the RTX3000 and RX6000 series were announced, I got the upgrade bug (mostly influenced by the want to move to 1440p). I was so set on rx6700 after seeing the 6900 and 6800 launches. I thought it was going to be a decent midrange card. I thought the pricing was going to be close to the 300ish range. I actually camped outside the Microcenter on launch night to get it, which was a cold and rainy chicago night. But prices were not released yet, embargos were lifted on launch day. I got a severe case of sticker shock when I was able to purchase one of the Sapphire reference models which ended up being just about 540 after tax. I was so disappointed, but with the chip shortage going on and everything else being sold out, I bought it anyways. The ONLY reason I dont really regret it was because i was able to sell my used 1060 for 300, effectively bringing my 6700 down to my 200-300 limit. 

I have been interested in upgrading again recently. I would like to move onto the AM5 platform. I would like to replace my 6700xt with something newer and more powerful. I am NOT ok with spending $700+ to do it. I understand that inflation and tariffs and yadda yadda happen, my expectation for pricing and purchasing power has to adjust to current climates. But with AMD specifically saying they are not producing any high end flagships, means these cards should fall in the mid range categories. I am NOT spending $700+ on a midrange card. 9070XT for $500 is my limit, might have to wait a few more months for a price drop like they always do, but it will get there eventually.

Author: @t_z1030
Content:
Radeon *really* does not seem to understand that its customer base is now completely limited to tech nerds and the *extremely* value-conscious. In other words, the people who will actually look at reliable review sources and make a cost-benefit analysis in their head before purchasing. Nvidia can get away with bad reviews because the schmucks who buy on brand recognition alone will always pick green without any research, i.e. exactly the attitude people used to have with Intel. When almost nobody would buy AMD it was the tech nerds who could see the value and potential in the early Ryzen CPUs, despite them being technically inferior to Intel's offerings at the time in a number of key ways. It was their experiences and word of mouth that gradually lifted the brand's reputation to where it is today. Now just about anyone on the street would be happy going AMD on the CPU side.

Radeon is now where AMD was in 2017. Regular Joes *do not* walk in off the street to buy a prebuilt and choose Radeon. Casual PC enjoyers *do not* choose Radeon for their next upgrade. Radeon need to pull a Ryzen and satisfy their core audience with inarguable value. If they screw up these launch reviews by pricing it too high AGAIN, then they will lose the only people left who'll give their product a chance. And then Radeon might as well close its doors.

Author: @klaudyw3
Content:
The worse part is that the NVIDIA - $50 doesn't even work correctly. If the performance was roughly the same, or $50 worse, it would make sense, but AFAIK a lot of the time it's not, it's worse than that. Throw in that NVIDIA has a lot more market share, what's the incentive to buy AMD, outside of the "Fuck NVIDIA!" reason? 

Instead of fucking around with expensive cards, marketing, etc. go the intel route and make some cards that most people can afford. AMD already has the experience, it's not going to hit a lot of the issues Intel ran into. They just need to find a niche they can make a dent in - something like $400 cards. Make the best thing you can make for that price point, and take a small(er) profit margin. All of the GPUs with defects, lower clocks, etc. can go towards the lower price points. Boom, market share. I have no idea if this would even lower their profits noticeably, a great buy at a low cost should see a lot more inventory moving compared to a meh buy at a high price.

For now i think AMD is just comfortable playing second fiddle to NVIDIA, hoping for a Ryzen-esque miracle sometime in the next 5 years. Short of that, they'll just slowly die out because they don't want to change anything.

Author: @Trae
Content:
Usually don't comment on vids in general but I've had some thoughts about the state of things for a while now.

AMD, for what it's worth, has made some very good hardware, especially with the RX7000 series, and It's all well and fine if the RX 9070(XT) has great hardware and also priced very well, and from what I've observed with friends who happen to use AMD GPUs, things like driver issues basically don't seem like a thing anymore, either.


All said though, it's going to take a lot more than *just* great hardware and pricing for AMD to be able to compete with NVIDIA at this point. Gaming is great and all, but if someone's going to dump $1000+ on a GPU, they should rightly expect the GPU to be capable of more than just gaming — people jump to NVIDIA as the first option because it's seen as the Swiss Army knife of the GPU space, and safe to assume that those GPUs will work with just about everything. I feel that developers for DCC pipeline software (Blender, Substance, Unity, Unreal etc.) seem to build for NVIDIA GPU support with everything else treated as more of an afterthought.

For example, the 7900XTX can be competitive with NVIDIA's high-end GPUs, like the 4080s and so on, but it literally took emulating NVIDIA's CUDA kernel on AMD's ROCm kernel stack to get there, and that's literally just comparing CUDA for CUDA. Things just get blown out of the water when NVIDIA's OptiX is brought into the picture — there's no contest whatsoever when the NVIDIA GPUs run at full tilt. Look at Blender's Open Data benchmarks — the top 25 entries in terms of performance are all NVIDIA, with the 7900XTX sitting 28th (using ZLUDA, no less, the first native implementation is further down the order still). Hell, *Apple* of all chipmakers is doing better than AMD. The biggest insult to injury? AMD is still being hamstrung with having RT acceleration tied up behind being an experimental option, and has been so for near 2 years now with no indication of whenever it'll be the default out of the box.

Gets even worse on Linux, where people can't even use the newer specs for HDMI, thus affecting monitor capabilities, because the HDMI Forum won't allow an open-source implementation.

It's a real shame at the state of the GPU space in general, and I'm rooting for AMD to make some genuine headway in making things better for everyone, and provide some real incentive for third parties to give a damn about providing genuine support for the hardware. Can only imagine how RDNA5 CUs on a bed of L3$ a la Zen 5's X3D implementation could perform...

Author: @desild5869
Content:
The real problem is RTG became so small there's a very good chance it can no longer afford to take on NVIDIA.
NVIDIA now makes 80% of their money from not-gaming and in gaming they took 90% of the market. This makes for a company with basically infinite technological and financial resources compared to RTG.

If RTG starts a price war by, let's say, selling the 9070 much lower than NVIDIA's price-x-performance line says it should cost, they risk upsetting NVIDIA. We already know what can happen in that case, NVIDIA is known to quickly rage-release much better revamped products or ramp up allocations for existing products and deeply drop prices.

Problem is, RTG would be nuked into zero profit (or even losses) by this move, killing their ability to finance R&D for future cards and pushing them into bankruptcy. Meanwhile, not only can NVIDIA easily afford much lower (even 0) profits from gaming cards with no impact on financing R&D for future products but due to their current tech superiority, they can lower prices far below what RTG can while STILL remaining profitable. They can literally suffocate RTG into bankruptcy with zero effort.

This is why RTG can't afford upsetting NVIDIA and why the best strategy for survival until they (and IF they ever) manage to produce a card so good its BOM is literally lower than NVIDIA's equivalent (while software and features are on par), is to price their card according to what NVIDIA says it should cost. That's why RTG cards are shit. It's the best they can do anymore. Their only option is to get out of the dGPU market or risk being taken out by a war with NVIDIA. There is no justification to risk shareholder money like that UNLESS you  think you can win. RDNA4 was pretty much born a loser from the moment it was announced. It does NOT have what it takes to fight NVIDIA. Expect underwhelming prices.

Author: @themomaw
Content: Everybody keeps saying that competition is good and necessary, okay cool. But here's a question. At what point should AMD give up? If you're committed to "competition at any cost", then you're not running a business. Competition needs to make financial sense or there is no point in doing it.  Gamers have already voted to give Nvidia 90% of the market, and they have a MASSIVE advantage. It's all well and good to say that AMD needs to offer a product that is better, while spending substantially less on R&D, *and* they can't put their price anywhere near the competition or people won't buy it...but how does sacrificing that much actually benefit AMD? Their final objective is to make money, not to apply downward pricing pressure on other companies. So again: At what point should we just accept that gamers do not want competition enough to actually support competition. They want Nvidia, and AMD should just give up. Because if the answer is "never" then you aren't having an honest conversation about what's going on here.

The problem with AMD's management is there is some investor or marketer or multiple of them that are making the statement, "You are leaving money on the table", every time someone recommends a cheaper price.  Those dumba... individuals don't understand their position with a bad public image.  It does not matter how epic of a GPU AMD can launch, there are too many customers that are fanatical towards Nvidia and won't care about any advancements from their GPUs.  AMD needs to one up Nvidia in as many areas as possible.

The focus AMD needs to look at is eroding that fanatical trust that several consumers have in Nvidia, as if Nvidia could do no wrong.  Now, I feel the hardware surveys are very misleading.  Nvidia has the discrete laptop market dominated, and those numbers can distort the image.  As much as everyone claims that the hardware surveys have different entries for Nvidia's laptop and desktop GPUs, that is utter BS.  Steam's Hardware Survey needs to permit filtering out all setups involving a laptop CPU and display numbers on verified desktop setups vs laptop setups.  It would be good for developers to know how many of their gamers are on laptops.  Laptops and desktops may run the same software, but they are 2 different demographics.

If AMD wants to pick up a few pieces, my recommendation involves hitting at Nvidia's PhysX 32-bit support.  Emulating PhysX is a part of fair competition.  Find features that Nvidia is abandoning and pick up the pieces.  People don't really like MultiFrame generation due to input situation.  Use "AI" to combine frames instead of extrapolating frames.

Author: @UncleTurboBeard
Content:
Thanks Steve,

I believe AMD has an opportunity to captialize on the perception of reliability, stability, and long-term customer support to win marketshare. AMD does not need to win the halo product performance crown. If AMD provides a solid performing card at a reasonable price with no newly introduced stability or driver issues, they will win hearts and minds and marketshare. Just as I no longer recommend Intel silicon for friends, family, and multi-million dollar server/workstation acquisitions at my company, I also am not going to recommend NVIDIA RTX5000 series. Right now, I'm begging for an alternative to the RTX5000 cards, because there are a lot of pending purchases that we had planned for this upgrade cycle. We've had to delay those acquisitions because we refuse to invest in an unreliabile product (something about dollars and downtime). 

Due to how terrible the situation is with RTX5000 series cards,  many enthusiasts/professionals in my situation (who make the purchasing decisions for both businesses and friends & family) are going to recommend the product that won't fail. Those factors absolutely overshadow any performance benefits of the RTX5000. I may purchase a 5090 for myself (for fun) sometime in the future because I have the technical ability to fix it myself if I need to. But, I absolutely will not recommend my friends, family, or business invest in a product that has a high likelyhood of failure, no matter the performance. I will be the one they call on for support, and it's my time and reputation on the line. 

There exists a Ryzen-like opportunity for AMD to win over GPU customers just as they did in the CPU space. The stars have aligned and the opportunity has literally been handed to AMD on a silver platter. Do not try to squeeze a much profit as possible this generation. Play the long game, give up the short-term profits in exchange for marketshare and mindshare. If you succeed, the future profits will explode just as they did for Ryzen and Epyc. If AMD screws this up, heads need to roll accross management and leadership in the company that are making these decisions. What does AMD have to lose? Less marketshare? Do not waste this opportunity.

Author: @kenshirogenjuro873
Content:
Emphasizing what I’ve said in a few places already:

The 9070XT has the same die size as the 7800XT.

It shares the same 256-bit bus.

It shares the same 16GB GDDR6 VRAM. It’s not newer. It’s not faster. There isn’t any more of it.

The 7800XT launched with all that for $500 *two* *years* *ago*

Now let’s back up another step and remember the 7800XT was really the 7700XT misbranded, as its N32 chip was the successor to the 6700XT’s N22 chip. That also was the same die size. And the 6700XT launched at $480. Noticing a trend?

Yeah…that’s right. The 8700X…er…9070XT die size is the same as the 6700XT. And it has the same VRAM as the 7800XT and 7900GRE. It’s not one iota larger or faster. Two years later.

I don’t know where AMD’s head is right now, but we can definitely confirm what they were initially thinking. It’s exactly the $400-600 range all the early leaks suggested beginning over a year ago.

I mean…let’s be clear this also seriously underscores how abusive Nvidia is *and* how gullible their buyers are…because this thing is going to be knocking on 5080 performance (that btw also has…the same die size) that their fool buyers are trampling each other over trying to pay $2000 for.

But there’s ZERO reason AMD can’t release the 9070XT and 9070 cards in the general price range of where the 7800XT, 7900GRE, and 6700XT did. We all *know* AMD has execs and shareholders expecting to leverage their sense of entitlement over this launch by demanding more money per card (they contributed nothing toward designing) while having done nothing but undermine Radeon’s mindshare the last half-dozen years with horrible pricing structures.

Personally I’m very much looking forward to these cards. But if the goal is marketshare most buyers just aren’t as open-minded as the 10-20% who are educated enough to objectively weigh Nvidia vs AMD *and* *then* *actually* *buy* *AMD* when it makes sense. AMD has to price as competitively as they can afford and they have plenty of ability to.

Content:
Honestly AMD, if the standard Raster performance of the RX 9070-XT matches the RTX 5070-Ti and the gap in Ray-Tracing performance is much closer this generation, then I will pay up to $649.99 for it. Remember AMD, this Nvidia GPU shortage is TEMPORARY. In a couple months, you WILL be able to buy a 5070-Ti 16GB at its $749.99 MSRP. Therefore, pricing too high because of GPU shortage/scalping prices is INVALID and nobody will buy your GPUs if you do it. And this advice comes from a current 7900-XTX owner, so you can trust this isn't biased against you.

As Steve says, you need CUSTOMERS right now, you need brand recognition, and you need to APPEAL TO GAMERS by offering a substantial lead over Nvidia in Performance-Per-Dollar Ratios across your entire RX 9000 series. If your Ray-Tracing performance is still nowhere near the 5070-Ti and you can only offer Raster performance, then the 9070-XT NEEDS to be priced BELOW $599.99. In conclusion AMD, the ONLY WAY that anyone will buy your GPU at ANY price point over $600, is that it BOTH matches or exceeds the performance of the RTX 5070-Ti 16GB in traditional rasterized graphics, and you need to come pretty close in Ray-Tracing performance as well, like I am talking - within 10% of the RT performance of the RTX 5070-Ti.

In short, if you do well - I will purchase an RX 9070-XT for the PC I am currently building for my girlfriend. She will be playing at 3440x1440p resolution, so performance equaling or very close to the RTX 5070-Ti 16GB would be perfect. However, if you do not do well, then I will be purchasing an RTX 5070-Ti 16GB when they are more readily available.
